title: Who Decides Which State Votes First?
hook: The order states vote in a presidential nominating contest isn't set by any constitution — it's a party rule, and parties rewrite it to change whose voters get courted first.
key_points: Nominating calendars are internal party rules, not constitutional or (mostly) statutory law — the party writes them and can change them.
NPR reports Democrats set South Carolina first for 2028, then Nevada, with New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia also holding early contests.
The party's stated reason for the new order was to prioritize Black and Latino voters early in the process.
Voting early confers outsized influence: early states winnow the field before most voters ever cast a ballot.
Candidates campaign hardest where they must win first, so calendar order shapes which issues get attention nationally.
content_html: Almost everything about a national election feels fixed by law: the date, the offices, who can vote. The order in which states pick a party's nominee is not. That's a party rule — written by the party, for the party, and rewritten when the party wants a different result.
extra_html:
NPR's Maham Javaid reported in July 2026 that Democrats approved a new calendar for 2028 putting South Carolina first, followed by Nevada, with New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia also holding early contests. The party's stated rationale was to prioritize Black and Latino voters early in the process.

The reason parties fight over this is that going first is worth far more than one state's share of the population. Early contests winnow: candidates who underperform run out of money and attention and drop out, so voters in later states choose from a field that has already been cut down. Campaigns respond by spending disproportionate time in the first states, which means those states' local concerns get a national hearing. Setting the order is therefore a way of deciding, in advance, which parts of a coalition candidates will have to speak to. (This describes U.S. party nominating practice; other democracies select candidates through party conventions, membership ballots, or leadership elections, with their own sequencing fights.)

related.hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.

related.title: Why Outsiders Keep Capturing 'Establishment' Parties
related.hook: Modern parties look powerful on television and weak up close — most have little real control over who runs under their banner. That gap is what lets outsider candidates walk in and take over.

related.title: Voter Turnout & Engagement
related.hook: Who shows up changes who wins. Turnout — the share of eligible people who actually vote — is one of the quiet forces shaping every election.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

flashcards.prompt: Who sets the order of states in a U.S. presidential nominating calendar?
flashcards.back_html: The political party itself, through internal rules — not the constitution. A party can reorder its own calendar between cycles.

flashcards.prompt: Why does going first give a state influence out of proportion to its size?

choices.text: Early contests winnow the field, so later voters choose from a list already narrowed
Early states are awarded extra delegates for voting first
A candidate who wins the first state is automatically nominated

flashcards.explanation_html: Weak performers drop out after early losses. By the time most voters participate, the realistic choices have already been cut down.

flashcards.prompt: Per NPR, what reason did Democrats give for putting South Carolina first in 2028?

choices.text: To prioritize Black and Latino voters early in the nominating process
To reduce the total cost of running a national campaign
To match the order used by the Republican Party

flashcards.explanation_html: Calendar order signals which parts of a coalition a party wants courted first — the stated rationale here was demographic representation early in the sequence.
